units: a notebook heads the list of recommended accessories
the lamp in use must carry a red filter to spare an eye adapted to the dark
the steady mount is described as the piece people skip most often
an instrument that shakes gives no usable image
the optical instrument ranks only fourth on the list
a cheap model is judged good enough to start with
two eyepieces of different magnifications are recommended
a star chart is needed to find your way among the stars
going out regularly counts for more than the quality of the gear
text: Want to watch the night sky without spending much? Start with a short list. A notebook comes first, because what you jot down beats what you half remember later. Next, a lamp with a red filter, which spares an eye that has already settled into the dark. Then the mount, the piece almost everyone skips and the one that decides everything: a shaky instrument shows you nothing worth looking at. The telescope itself ranks only fourth, and a cheap model will carry you through your first months. Pack two eyepieces as well, one to sweep wide fields, the other to pull in a detail. Add a star chart, on paper or on a screen, or you will drift from one point of light to the next without naming any of it. Gear counts for less than habit. Go out often, even briefly, and your eye will learn on its own what moves and what stays put.

units: the turning part of the building stayed jammed on opening night

text: On opening night the dome flatly refused to turn. Guests stood about on the terrace with their drinks while two technicians climbed the inner ladder to look at the mechanism. They found a strip of metal wedged in the circular rail, dropped there at some forgotten moment. One of them worked it loose with a screwdriver, and the other greased the gearing. Half an hour later the whole frame began to swing around again, with a low rumble that the crowd took for thunder. The shutter slid open on a clear sky, and the head of the observatory, plainly relieved, put together a speech of three sentences on the spot. What he left out, and what the local paper printed the next morning, was where the metal came from: a bolt the fitters had forgotten, which had nearly wrecked an evening two years in the making.

units: your hands must be dry and free of jewelry before you start
a greasy mark attracts the particles that scratch the surface
the work is done in a closed room to avoid drafts
the disk is rinsed in lukewarm water with no cloth at all
fabric moves the grains around instead of carrying them off
every grain shifted digs a groove that scatters the light of the stars
the water must run off by itself before the rim is dried
repeated washing damages the reflecting layer faster than the surrounding air
text: Before you so much as lay a hand on the mirror, dry it and take off every ring. A smear of grease pulls in dust, and dust will scratch the surface the moment anything rubs across it. Set the instrument down flat in a closed room, because one draft brings back onto the glass everything you have just cleared away. Rinse the disk under lukewarm water and use no cloth at all. Fabric shoves the grains around instead of carrying them off, and every grain you shift leaves a tiny groove that will scatter the light of the stars. Let the water run off by itself, then blot the rim alone with soft paper. If marks are still there, do not try again tomorrow. Wait out a whole season, because washing too often wears down the thin reflecting layer far faster than a year of open air ever will.

units: maneuvers meant to avoid a collision are becoming more frequent
the cause lies in the buildup of debris in low orbit
a tiny fragment can punch through a reinforced wall because of its speed
every impact produces new fragments whose course turns unpredictable
the phenomenon therefore keeps itself going
the first answer is to catalogue the objects by radar
the second requires a fuel reserve to bring the craft back down at the end of its mission
the third answer, still at the test stage, plans to capture one bulky piece of debris
text: Satellite operators report a steady rise in avoidance maneuvers. Behind it lies a growing crowd of debris in low orbit: rocket parts, bolts, flakes of paint, all traveling fast enough that a chip the size of a fingernail can punch through an armored wall. Every impact breeds fresh fragments, and their paths in turn grow hard to predict, so the whole problem quietly keeps itself going. Space agencies are currently trying three answers. The first is to catalogue what is up there by radar, so that close approaches can be seen coming. The second requires every future craft to hold back enough fuel to drop itself toward the atmosphere once its mission ends. The third, still on the test bench, sends up a chaser to grab one bulky piece with a net or a harpoon and pull it out of orbit.

units: two neighboring circular hollows show opposite appearances

its floor is lined with fine particles stirred by later impacts
the more recent one has a crisp wall cut into terraces

both formations belong to the same natural satellite
text: Two neighboring craters offer the patient observer two opposite kinds of relief. The older one has a rounded rim, worn nearly flat, and a floor buried under fine dust that later impacts have stirred over and over. The younger raises a crisp wall cut into a stack of terraces, and its floor still holds an untouched central peak. The contrast does not stop at the outline. Nothing bright survives around the older bowl, while a web of pale rays reaches an enormous distance out around the younger, marking the stuff thrown clear at the moment of impact. Grazing light widens the gap further. The old basin sinks into one flat tone, and its neighbor cuts a hard, stretched shadow across the ground. One and the same natural satellite therefore carries two faces side by side, ages apart.

units: the text asks whether lit signs should go dark after midnight
the writer refuses to treat the subject from the sky watchers' side alone

the writer sees in that loss a landmark shared by all of humanity
not one of the arguments put forward calls for complete darkness
the conclusion argues for aimed lighting, dimmed at night, and for protected areas
text: Should lit signs go dark after midnight? The question deserves more than one angle, and the sky watchers cannot own it. Start with money: light aimed down at the ground burns less than a beam scattered upward. Then health, since steady artificial brightness breaks the sleep of people living nearby and throws migrating birds off their course. Last comes the cultural case, the one that looks weakest at first glance. A whole generation now reaches adulthood without once having seen the milky band of our own galaxy, and with it we give up a landmark every human being used to share. Not one of these arguments calls for total darkness. What they call for is plain: lighting that points where it is needed, dimmed past a certain hour, and protected stretches where the sky stays black.

genre: portrait / biographie (personne désignée par son rôle)

her last mirror is still in service and the team using it does not know who she was
text: She came into the optical workshop as a cleaner, very young, with no diploma and nobody to speak for her. The foreman handed her buckets and sawdust and nothing else. One evening she picked up on her own a glass disk that an apprentice had spoiled, and she polished it until daylight. The next morning the foreman held the surface up to a lamp, looked a long while, then moved her to a bench. She never left it. She learned to feel under her thumb a hollow that no device of the day could measure, and the most delicate orders ended up at her station. Near the end of her working life she trained two apprentices, repeating one rule to them: never force the glass. The last mirror she polished still serves under a mountain dome, and the team who use it have no idea whose hands shaped it.

units: the show traces the making of a star and then its end
the images are judged unusually sharp
that quality comes from the scanning of genuine archive plates
the pace never slows at any point
the lack of pauses ends up blunting the wonder of the audience
the unbroken music piles on emphasis that serves no purpose
the narration explains too much and leaves nothing to imagine
the reviewer holds that a shorter show would have left a deeper mark
text: The show impresses from the opening minute, and that is exactly what ends up working against it. The seats tilt back, the vault lights up, and in one sitting you watch a star take shape, swell, then collapse. The images are unusually sharp, because the team scanned real archive plates before setting them in motion. But the pace never eases off for a moment, and that missing breath turns the whole thing around: once one cosmic disaster follows straight on from another, you simply stop being amazed. The music runs without a break as well, piling emphasis on a subject that needed none. The narration, for its part, explains far too much and leaves you nothing to picture on your own. A shorter show, broken by silence and by a sky holding still, would have stayed with me longer.

units: the letter arrived the day before the sun was covered over

the writer asks for an account of what was felt
text: Your letter reached me the day before the eclipse, and I read it standing out in the cold. You tell me you are giving up on watching, having no instrument and, as you put it, no nerve. Let me offer you something else. Take a piece of card, prick it with a pin, hold it at arm's length over a white sheet, and the sun will draw its own thin sickle there, narrowing while you watch, with nothing risked on your side. If cloud moves in, stay where you are. A pale ring may then close around the disk, and that circle alone is worth the walk. As for having no instrument, it forces you to look around you rather than up. The color of the ground shifts, the birds go quiet, the air turns cold all at once. None of that costs a thing. Write and tell me what you felt, not what you thought you were supposed to feel.

units: the question bears on the difference between two rings seen around a heavenly body
the distinction lies in the matter crossed and in the optical mechanism

those crystals bend the incoming light by one fixed angle

the second ring forms in low cloud full of droplets or in a veil of fine particles
it comes from diffraction rather than from bending
that ring is narrow, colored and pressed close against the disk
its width depends on the size of the particles
a wide pale ring points to ice, a tight iridescent ring points to drops or grains
text: A reader asks what really separates a halo from a corona, given that both of them wrap the disk in a ring. The answer lies in what the light passes through on its way and in the optics at work. A halo forms in very high cloud built of six-sided ice crystals, which bend the incoming light by one fixed angle. The ring that results is wide, whitish, and comes out much the same size every time. A corona forms lower down, in cloud loaded with droplets or in a thin veil of dust, and it comes from diffraction rather than bending. That ring is narrow, colored, pressed close against the disk, and its width depends on how big the particles are. So here is a simple rule you can carry outdoors with you: a broad pale ring points to ice, a tight iridescent one points to drops or grains.
